body:
How to write an article with Claude without it sounding generated: the step-by-step procedure. The difference between a text written with Claude's help and one that clearly sounds AI-generated does not lie in the tool used, but in the steps the writer follows before, during and after the conversation with the assistant.

The procedure below starts from a written brief, goes through concrete requests to Claude and ends with a mandatory manual edit. Each step solves a specific problem, not just the vague requirement to sound "more human".

How to write an article with Claude without it sounding generated: the step-by-step procedure

A command like "write an article about X" almost always produces a generic text, however capable the model behind it. The guide below shows how to use Claude for writing blog articles that go unnoticed as AI-assisted, because they follow a multi-step procedure, not a single command.

Each step below can be checked as you write, rather than being just a general recommendation.

Why AI-generated text is easy to spot

A generic text often starts with a sentence that redefines the subject in different words without adding anything new. The following paragraphs string together correct statements, but ones that are valid for any company in any field, not for the one being written about.

The pattern repeats at sentence level too: transition connectors used in every paragraph, such as "in addition" or "however", and conclusions that summarise the introduction in other words. The reader feels they have already read the article, even on the first read-through.

The signals below appear most often in an unedited text:

  • Every section has the same length and the same sentence structure, whatever the topic.
  • Statements stay general: "it is important", "it matters a lot", with no concrete example attached.
  • There is no verifiable figure, no date, no first-hand experience from the author.
  • The conclusion repeats the introduction, instead of adding a next step for the reader.

These signals matter beyond the reader's perception. Google also evaluates content by how much new information it adds compared with what already exists online, and the E-E-A-T audit tool shows exactly where first-hand experience is missing from a text.

An example: from a vague prompt to a specific paragraph

The difference between the steps below and an ordinary command is best seen through a complete example, from prompt to result.

A vague prompt sounds like this: "write a paragraph about the importance of site speed for SEO". The answer, almost guaranteed, begins with "site speed matters for user experience and for ranking in search engines", followed by statements valid for any site in any field.

A prompt built following the procedure below looks different: "write a paragraph about site speed, starting from the fact that I enabled the cache in cPanel and disabled three unused plugins; explain what exactly changed in concrete terms for the visitor, not the general effect of speed". The example above is hypothetical, but the mechanism is real: the more verifiable details the prompt contains, the less room the answer has for general wording.

The same logic applies to any technical topic covered on a blog, from server configuration to explanations about the Google algorithm. The concrete detail in the prompt becomes the concrete detail in the text, not the other way round.

Step 1: prepare a brief before you open Claude

The brief comes before any conversation with Claude, not the other way round. It contains the target keyword, the search intent, the required structure by section and the article's mandatory internal links.

Without a brief, the writer asks Claude to choose the angle of the text itself, and the result tends towards the most common angle possible, the one already covered by hundreds of similar articles. With a brief, the first request sent to the model already contains the right constraints.

A useful brief also answers a simple question: what does the writer know about this subject, from direct experience, that Claude cannot know? The answer becomes the core of the article, not an addition at the end.

If you are not sure which writing tool to use beforehand, the comparison between Claude and ChatGPT shows the differences relevant for a company in Romania, including for content writing.

Step 2: give Claude your own facts, not just the subject

Genericness appears because the model receives an empty subject and fills the hole with what is statistically probable, that is, the most common wording in the material it was trained on. The solution is to fill the hole yourself, before asking for the final text.

In the prompt, include real steps from your work process, a concrete situation met with a client (without data that identifies them) or a figure you can back up with a source. Claude organises and words these facts, but it does not invent them if you do not give them.

For anyone who has not used Claude at all yet, the basic explanation of what Claude AI is and how to use it clarifies the minimum concepts before this step.

In practice, the own facts useful for a blog article usually fall into one of three categories: a step in the work process that you repeat often, a frequent mistake met with clients and the way you corrected it, or a direct observation from a tool you use daily. Any of them makes the difference compared with a text written with no input information.

Never ask Claude for a figure or a study that you cannot verify separately. The model can generate a plausible number that is not backed by a real source, and publishing it remains the writer's responsibility.

Step 3: ask for a structure before the full text

Instead of a single command asking for the complete article, the first prompt asks only for an outline: the H2 and H3 sections, the main idea of each and a word target. The outline can be read in a few seconds and corrected before any paragraph has been written.

Only after the structure is approved is each section requested separately, with the own facts added from the previous step. Text generated in small pieces keeps a distinct thread more easily, unlike a whole article requested in a single command.

You will find examples of prompts for each stage, from the initial outline to the conclusion section, in the article with prompt examples for Claude. For variants on your exact subject, the AI prompt generator on the site starts from a fillable template.

What an approved outline looks like before the final text

A good outline lists each H2 section on one line, with a single sentence about what it contains and a word target alongside. It does not yet contain final sentences, only reference points that you can move or delete.

If a section in the outline repeats another one above it, this is seen immediately and it is removed before you have spent time on a whole paragraph. The same quick check also shows whether a section that the brief explicitly required is missing.

Step 4: manually rewrite the paragraphs that sound generic

The manual edit is not optional, however good the prompt was. It fixes exactly the patterns described earlier, the ones the reader recognises instantly.

On rereading, check each paragraph against a short list of questions:

  • Does the opening sentence bring new information or just rename the section title?
  • Is there at least one concrete, verifiable detail specific to your business?
  • Do the transition connectors repeat identically in every paragraph?
  • Does the last sentence of the section add something or just summarise what has already been said?

Paragraphs that fail any of these questions are rewritten manually, not requested again from Claude with the prompt "make it less generic". Direct rewriting is faster and stays under your control.

Step 5: check the facts, figures and links before publication

The last step is a check separate from the style edit, focused strictly on accuracy. Every statement that sounds like a verifiable fact goes through a real source, not through the model's memory.

The links suggested by Claude are checked one by one, because the model may suggest a plausible address that does not exist or that leads to the wrong page. The rule stays the same as for any article written without AI: internal links lead only to pages that are already published, not to imagined or scheduled pages.

A quick final pass covers four points, in this order:

  • Every figure or date in the text has a source you can show, not just "that is what Claude said".
  • Every internal link leads to a real address, checked directly in the browser, not just assumed correct.
  • Technical terms explained on first appearance remain correct after the manual rewriting of the paragraphs.
  • No sentence promises a guaranteed result, such as a particular position in Google.

The last pass through the text also confirms that no trace of the conversation with the model remains, such as uncleaned instructions or wording like "as a language model". The final text must read naturally, as if it had been written entirely by the writer.

The complete procedure, with a written brief, own facts, an approved outline, manual editing and a final check, turns Claude into a tool for assisted writing, not an invisible author. For pages that support this type of content on a blog, the article on the complete Claude guide complements the details on installation and configuration, and teams that want a process built for them can look at the SEO optimisation page or the technical SEO one.

Applied consistently, the procedure above shortens writing time without shortening the quality of the text delivered. The difference is not visible in the first article, but after a few months, when the series of published texts looks consistent, with verifiable own facts in every piece, not only in those written without deadline pressure.
